title: Teaching
text: I teach statistics and data science at St. Lawrence University, emphasizing statistical reasoning, practical tools, and learning through real problems.

title: Teaching
text:
Regularly Taught Courses
STAT 113 — Applied Statistics
An introduction to statistical reasoning and inference.
STAT/DATA 234 — Foundations of Data Science
Data wrangling, visualization, and reproducible analysis using the R tidyverse sute of tools.
STAT 213 — Applied Regression
Linear and Logistic regression modeling.
STAT 226 — Statistical Design and Analysis for Data Collection
Sampling methods and experimental design, from data collection to statistical inference.
STAT 313 — Advanced Linear Models
Statistical models extending beyond ordinary linear regression - such as general linear models and multilevel models.

title: Ivan Ramler
text:
Professor of Statistics and Data Science
St. Lawrence University
I am a Professor of Statistics and Data Science in the Department of Mathematics, Computer Science, and Statistics at St. Lawrence University. My professional interests include statistics education, sports analytics, and statistical applications to the biological and environmental sciences.
Much of my scholarly activity focuses on creating educational resources that make statistical thinking accessible and relevant. This includes my work with the SCORE Network and contributions to What’s Going On in This Graph?, a feature of The New York Times Learning Network.





For more information, see my projects, teaching, or curriculum vitae and contact details.

title: Projects
text: My work includes developing statistics education materials, contributing to scholarship about teaching and learning with data, and applications to other fields (mainly sports and the environmental sciences). Below are a few ongoing activities and areas of interest.

title: Projects
text:
Statistics education and public engagement

SCORE Network
I work with the SCORE Network, an academic–industry collaboration that develops and shares educational resources using sports to teach statistics and data science.
In addition to serving as an editor for the Network, I develop educational modules, often in collaboration with undergraduate students. Together, we have published several SCORE Modules.

What’s Going On in This Graph?
I an a free-lance writer and editor for The New York Times Learning Network feature, What’s Going On in This Graph?.
What’s Going On in This Graph? is a weekly feature from The New York Times Learning Network and the American Statistical Association that encourages students to explore real-world data visualizations. Through a series of open-ended questions, students practice interpreting graphs, identifying patterns, and communicating their observations.






Selected WGOITG Contributions






W.N.B.A. Players’ Compensation — Examines W.N.B.A. player compensation and revenue sharing compared with the N.B.A.
Homeowners Insurance — Maps where insurance companies are increasingly declining to renew homeowners’ policies.
Butterflies — Explores changes in butterfly populations across species from 2000 to 2020.






Esports Analytics
One of my primary research interests is applying statistical methods to competitive video games, particularly League of Legends. My work has examined topics such as player behavior, team composition, competitive strategies, and gender differences in player performance. Much of this research involves analyzing large datasets of competitive matches to better understand what contributes to success in these games.
My esports research has also provided opportunities to collaborate with undergraduate students and explore statistical questions that connect my professional interests with my enthusiasm for gaming. This work has resulted in several conference publications, an invited book chapter, and a Best Paper Award at the 2017 International Conference on the Foundations of Digital Games.






Selected Esports Publications






Identifying and Evaluating Successful Non-Meta Strategies (2017) — Investigates unconventional competitive strategies in League of Legends. Recipient of the FDG 2017 Best Paper Award.
Gender Differences in League of Legends (2021) — Examines differences in gameplay and performance using large-scale match data.
The Rise of the Bots (2015) — Studies automated player behavior in online gaming.
Champion Usage (2015) — Investigates patterns in character selection and usage in League of Legends.
